cards.front: Why are most big bodies made of many small cells instead of one giant cell?
cards.back: If a cell grows in every direction, its surface falls behind its inside, and its middle gets farther away. Many small cells keep plenty of surface and can share the jobs.
cards.quote: But if a cell grows in every direction, its surface falls behind its inside, and its middle gets farther away.

cards.front: For a cube-shaped model cell that keeps its shape, doubling the width makes the surface 4 times bigger but the inside {{c1::8 times}} bigger.
cards.back: So the surface for each small cube of inside is halved.
cards.quote: doubling the width makes the surface 4 times bigger but the inside 8 times bigger
cards.section: Explain: why not one giant cell?

cards.front: A cube-shaped model cell is 8 small cubes wide. How much surface does each small cube of inside get? (Surface = 6 × width × width; inside = width × width × width.)
cards.back: Surface = 6 × 8 × 8 = 384 squares. Inside = 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 small cubes. 384 ÷ 512 = 0.75 square for each small cube, less than one.
cards.quote: 0.75: 6 × 8 × 8 = 384 squares of surface for 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 small cubes of inside, less than one square each.
cards.section: Explain: why not one giant cell?

cards.front: Some nerve cells reach about a metre long. How can a cell that big still get materials to all of its inside?
cards.back: It grows long but stays thin, so no part of its inside is far from the surface.
cards.quote: some nerve cells reach about a metre but stay thin, so no part of the inside is far from the surface.
cards.section: Explain: why not one giant cell?

cards.front: A {{c1::unicellular}} organism, such as most bacteria and Paramecium, is just one cell.
cards.back: Many cells make a multicellular organism, such as you or an oak tree.
cards.quote: A unicellular organism, such as most bacteria and Paramecium, is just one cell.
cards.section: Explain: one cell does every job

cards.front: A Paramecium has no tissues or organs. How does it still carry out every life process?
cards.back: Its one cell does every job, using different parts of that cell for different jobs. The parts work together as a system.
cards.quote: Key idea: A unicellular organism carries out every life process inside one cell, using different parts of that cell for different jobs.
cards.section: Explain: one cell does every job

cards.front: Name the five levels of organization in a body like yours, from smallest to largest.
cards.back: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
cards.quote: Key idea: In many multicellular organisms, such as you, cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems, so each level does part of the work.

cards.front: A leaf is built from several different tissues working together. Which level of organization is a leaf, and why?
cards.back: An organ, like your heart. Different tissues working together make an organ. In a plant the levels run cells, tissues, leaf, shoot system.
cards.quote: A leaf is built from several different tissues working together.

cards.front: Why can damage to the heart's tissue harm the whole body, not just the heart?
cards.back: The levels depend on each other. If heart tissue is damaged, the whole body can suffer.
cards.quote: And they depend on each other: if heart tissue is damaged, the whole body can suffer.

cards.front: Does every multicellular animal have tissues, organs and organ systems? Give an example.
cards.back: No. Trichoplax, a tiny ocean animal, has several kinds of cells but no organs.
cards.quote: Trichoplax, a tiny ocean animal, has several kinds of cells but no organs.

cards.front: When specialized cells each do part of an organism's work, sharing the work this way is called {{c1::division of labor}}.
cards.quote: Sharing the work this way is division of labor.
cards.section: Explain: a shape for every job

cards.front: What is a specialized cell?
cards.back: A cell whose shape and parts fit it to one kind of job, such as a red blood, nerve or muscle cell.
cards.quote: Key idea: A specialized cell has a shape and parts that fit its job.
cards.section: Explain: a shape for every job

cards.front: Why is an arm muscle cell packed with mitochondria?
cards.back: Mitochondria release energy from food, and that energy powers the muscle cell's pulling.
cards.quote: These cell parts release energy from food, which powers the cell's pulling.
cards.section: Explain: a shape for every job

cards.front: A root hair cell takes in water from the soil. Should it be short and round, or long and thin? Why?
cards.back: Long and thin. A tube growing between soil grains puts more surface against the soil, where water comes in.
cards.quote: Long and thin: a tube growing between soil grains puts more surface against the soil, where water comes in.
cards.section: Explain: a shape for every job

cards.front: Compare an elephant and a mouse. Predict how a liver cell, and a nerve cell reaching from the spine to the foot, differ between them.
cards.back: The liver cells are not much different in size; the elephant just has far more. The nerve cell is longer in the elephant, because it must reach farther.
cards.why: Bigger mammals mostly have more cells, not bigger ones; a few kinds, like nerve cells, do grow larger.
cards.quote: a nerve cell reaching from the spine to the foot must be longer in a longer animal.
cards.section: Elaborate: more cells, more kinds of cells?

cards.front: A kind of cell (scientists say {{c1::cell type}}) is a group of cells that share a shape, parts and job, such as red blood cells.
cards.quote: A kind of cell (scientists say cell type) is a group of cells that share a shape, parts and job, such as red blood cells.
cards.section: Elaborate: more cells, more kinds of cells?

cards.front: Hydra has about 15 kinds of cells. Volvox carteri has 2. How many times more kinds of cells does Hydra have?
cards.quote: How many times more kinds of cells does Hydra have than Volvox carteri?
cards.section: Elaborate: more cells, more kinds of cells?

cards.front: A student tests whether adding salt to the water changes how often a Paramecium's contractile vacuole empties. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control.
cards.back: Independent: the amount of salt added (such as 0, 0.1 and 0.2 g per 100 mL). Dependent: how many times the vacuole empties in 60 seconds. Control: spring water with no salt added.
cards.quote: Control: spring water with no salt added.

cards.front: Volvox aureus has several hundred cells and 2 kinds. Volvox carteri has about 2,000 cells and 2 kinds. Trichoplax has a few hundred cells and 4 kinds. Is "more cells, more kinds of cells" a rule or a trend?
cards.back: A trend. Kinds tend to rise with cells, but adding cells did not add kinds in the two Volvox rows, and Trichoplax has fewer cells but more kinds than Volvox carteri.
cards.why: The numbers are rough: guesses from body size are good only to within about ten times, and the count of kinds depends on how finely cells are sorted.
cards.quote: kinds tend to rise with cells, but far more slowly.
cards.section: Elaborate: more cells, more kinds of cells?

cards.front: Use the cube model and division of labor together to explain why your body is trillions of small cells grouped into levels.
cards.back: A cell that grows in every direction and keeps its shape leaves less surface for each bit of inside, so without special features a giant cell may not move materials to its middle fast enough. Many small cells keep enough surface and can split the jobs, forming tissues, organs and organ systems shaped for their jobs.
cards.quote: use the cube numbers to explain why your body is trillions of small cells, grouped into levels and shaped for their jobs.
